name: Acute alcohol intoxication
definition: Dose-dependent acute central nervous system effects of ethanol.
mechanism: GABAergic/glutamatergic and broader neural effects reduce inhibition, psychomotor control, working memory, and response control.
behavioralConsequences: Impaired reaction time, working memory, response inhibition, coordination, judgment and risk assessment at sufficient dose.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change messaging or consent delivered while intoxicated may not be encoded or acted upon reliably.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Dose, drinking history, tolerance, sex/body composition, food, and context matter.
measurementIndicators: Breath/blood alcohol; observed impairment; dose/time
caveats: Alcohol does not uniformly increase aggression/risk; social context and expectancy strongly moderate behavior.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with norms, peers, incentives, environment, and sleep.

name: Acute caffeine stimulation
definition: Adenosine receptor antagonism following caffeine consumption.
mechanism: Reduces sleep pressure signals and increases alertness, vigilance, and reaction speed.
behavioralConsequences: Improved alertness and some attention/performance, especially when sleep deprived; high doses can increase jitteriness/anxiety and disrupt later sleep.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can temporarily offset sleepiness but not fully restore sleep-loss deficits; timing may alter subsequent behavior through sleep.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Dose, habitual use, withdrawal, timing, and sleep status matter.
measurementIndicators: Dose/time; caffeine intake history; performance; sleep timing
caveats: Do not treat caffeine as a substitute for sleep; some benefits reflect withdrawal reversal.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep debt, anxiety, stress, and shift work.

name: Acute hypoxia / reduced oxygen availability
definition: Reduced inspired or arterial oxygen sufficient to challenge cerebral oxygenation.
mechanism: Lower oxygen availability can impair neural energy metabolism and cognitive performance, especially at greater severity/duration.
behavioralConsequences: Slower reaction, poorer attention/executive function and memory at sufficient hypoxic dose; motor performance may degrade.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Training, communication, and decision support should be simplified under significant hypoxia.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Altitude, aviation, confined environments, illness; magnitude depends on saturation, acclimatization, task, and duration.
measurementIndicators: SpO2; arterial blood gas; altitude; inspired oxygen fraction
caveats: Mild hypoxia does not uniformly impair all tasks; dose and acclimatization matter.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with exertion, sleep, respiratory disease, temperature, and fatigue.

name: Acute infection / sickness-behavior state
definition: Coordinated behavioral and physiological response to infection or immune activation, often including fatigue, reduced activity, appetite change, sleepiness, and social withdrawal.
mechanism: Pro-inflammatory cytokines signal the brain and reorganize motivation toward energy conservation and recovery.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced exploration/activity, fatigue, appetite change, social withdrawal, impaired concentration.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavioral demands may be deprioritized during illness; reduced participation can be adaptive rather than noncompliant.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Severity and pathogen vary; fever is not required.
measurementIndicators: Symptoms; temperature; inflammatory markers; diagnosis/context
caveats: Do not pathologize adaptive sickness behavior or infer motivation from activity reduction.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with social support, work policies, information, medication, and resource access.

name: Acute injury / temporary physical impairment
definition: Temporary bodily damage that limits movement, dexterity, endurance, or sensory function.
mechanism: Pain, inflammation, immobilization, and reduced motor capacity constrain action possibilities.
behavioralConsequences: Avoidance, compensatory strategies, slower task execution, reduced range of feasible behaviors.
behaviorChangeRelevance: A desired behavior may be motivationally intact but physically impossible or costly; intervention must distinguish capability from motivation.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Type and severity of injury determine effects.
measurementIndicators: Clinical exam; range of motion; strength; gait; functional task performance
caveats: Do not infer unwillingness from reduced performance when capability is impaired.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with environmental accessibility, social assistance, technology, and institutional accommodations.

name: Acute nicotine exposure
definition: Acute nicotinic acetylcholine receptor stimulation from nicotine.
mechanism: Nicotine increases arousal and can improve attention/working-memory performance, particularly in deprived or dependent users.
behavioralConsequences: Short-term changes in alertness and attention; cardiovascular activation.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can transiently alter performance, but apparent benefits in dependent users may largely reverse withdrawal.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Non-smoker effects, dose, tolerance, and delivery method vary.
measurementIndicators: Nicotine dose; cotinine for exposure (not acute impairment); heart rate; user dependence
caveats: Do not present nicotine as a safe cognitive enhancer; dependence and cardiovascular harms matter.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with withdrawal, stress, social norms, and delivery technology.

name: Acute pain
definition: Short-duration nociceptive experience that competes for attention and motivates protection or escape.
mechanism: Nociceptive and salience systems capture attention and alter motor planning, valuation, and threat processing.
behavioralConsequences: Attention interference, avoidance, reduced working capacity, protective behavior, altered movement.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can dominate behavior and reduce engagement with non-urgent messages or tasks; pain control may be prerequisite for change.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend on intensity, controllability, location, meaning, and prior pain history.
measurementIndicators: Pain ratings; quantitative sensory testing; behavioral interference measures
caveats: Pain is subjective and context-sensitive; intensity is not the only determinant of behavior.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with fear, prior experience, social support, medication, and physical environment.

name: Acute physiological stress response
definition: Short-term activation of stress physiology in response to challenge or threat.
mechanism: HPA-axis and sympathetic-adrenomedullary activation changes arousal, attention allocation, memory retrieval, and valuation.
behavioralConsequences: Can narrow attention, alter risk-taking and learning, shift decisions under uncertainty, and prioritize threat-relevant action.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May either facilitate simple/urgent responses or degrade complex deliberation; intervention design should consider arousal level and task complexity.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend on stressor controllability, timing relative to decision, sex, baseline traits, and task domain.
measurementIndicators: Heart rate/HRV; blood pressure; salivary cortisol; alpha-amylase; catecholamine proxies
caveats: Stress does not have a single directional effect on risk or performance.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with threat framing, uncertainty, social evaluation, time pressure, and prior trauma.

name: Acute systemic inflammatory signaling
definition: Transient elevation of systemic inflammatory mediators from infection, injury, or experimental immune challenge.
mechanism: Cytokine-to-brain signaling alters reward, fatigue, mood, social motivation, and some cognitive processes.
behavioralConsequences: Fatigue, reduced reward sensitivity, altered social approach/withdrawal, impaired performance in some cognitive domains.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can transiently change responsiveness to incentives and willingness to expend effort.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects vary by inflammatory stimulus and individual susceptibility.
measurementIndicators: CRP; IL-6; TNF; experimental endotoxin; clinical inflammation markers
caveats: Inflammatory biomarkers are nonspecific; a single CRP value does not explain behavior.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with stress, sleep, obesity/metabolism, infection, and social context.

name: Acute THC/cannabis intoxication
definition: Acute central effects following intoxicating cannabinoid exposure, especially THC.
mechanism: CB1 receptor activation alters attention, memory encoding, psychomotor function, and time perception.
behavioralConsequences: Impaired learning/working memory, attention, reaction time and psychomotor performance; anxiety or altered perception in some users.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Complex instructions, driving, or high-precision behavior may be impaired during acute intoxication.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend on THC dose, CBD ratio, tolerance, route, and time since use.
measurementIndicators: Time/dose; toxicology with limitations; performance assessment
caveats: Detection of THC does not equal current impairment; chronic-use effects differ from acute intoxication.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with expectation, social setting, alcohol, anxiety, and task demands.

name: Acute total sleep deprivation
definition: Extended wakefulness sufficient to eliminate a normal sleep episode.
mechanism: Homeostatic sleep pressure and altered cortical/subcortical network function reduce vigilance, executive control, working memory, and response stability.
behavioralConsequences: Slower responses, attentional lapses, poorer working memory/executive control, greater performance variability and errors.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can reduce ability to notice, understand, remember, or execute a requested behavior; may increase reliance on habits and salient cues.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects vary by task, duration awake, circadian phase, stimulant use, and individual vulnerability.
measurementIndicators: Sleep/wake history; actigraphy; polysomnography; psychomotor vigilance; subjective sleepiness
caveats: Do not infer global incompetence from sleep loss; some tasks are more resilient than others.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts strongly with time pressure, stress, workload, information complexity, and technological alerting.

name: Adolescent neurodevelopmental stage
definition: Adolescent period of ongoing maturation in control, reward, social, and affective neural systems.
mechanism: Developmental imbalance/specialization across reward, social salience, and control systems changes context sensitivity.
behavioralConsequences: Heightened peer/social sensitivity, exploration, reward responsiveness, and variable risk-taking depending on context.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Interventions may work differently when social identity, immediate rewards, and peer context are highly salient.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Not all adolescents are risk-seeking; context effects are central.
measurementIndicators: Age/developmental stage; executive and reward tasks; pubertal stage
caveats: Avoid simplistic 'immature prefrontal cortex' narratives.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts strongly with peers, culture, autonomy, sleep timing, and institutions.

name: Adverse circadian phase / time-of-day vulnerability
definition: Normal within-day variation in alertness and cognitive capacity produced by circadian phase.
mechanism: Circadian oscillations influence arousal and cognitive efficiency, creating predictable peaks and troughs.
behavioralConsequences: Time-of-day differences in attention, reaction time, inhibition, and decision performance.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change prompts, training, assessments, or high-stakes choices may perform differently depending on timing.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend on chronotype, sleep pressure, light exposure, and task type.
measurementIndicators: Clock time; chronotype; sleep history; melatonin phase when available
caveats: Do not universalize 'morning is better'; optimal time varies by chronotype and task.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with work schedules, age, chronotype, caffeine, and light.

name: Alcohol withdrawal
definition: Physiological state after abrupt reduction of heavy/prolonged alcohol use.
mechanism: Neuroadaptation produces autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and in severe cases seizures/delirium.
behavioralConsequences: Agitation, impaired concentration, autonomic symptoms, sleep disruption; severe withdrawal can be life-threatening.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change or decision demands are secondary to medical stabilization in significant withdrawal.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Relevant only in physiologically dependent users; severity varies.
measurementIndicators: Withdrawal scales (e.g. CIWA-Ar); alcohol history; autonomic signs; clinical assessment
caveats: Potential medical emergency; not a routine motivational problem.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with stress, social support, access to care, medication, and environment.

name: Anemia / reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
definition: Reduced hemoglobin or red-cell capacity sufficient to impair oxygen delivery and increase fatigue.
mechanism: Lower oxygen delivery and compensatory cardiovascular strain can reduce endurance and may affect cognition.
behavioralConsequences: Fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance; observational evidence links anemia with higher cognitive impairment risk.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May reduce physical and cognitive capacity to perform or sustain new behaviors.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Cause matters: iron deficiency, bleeding, chronic disease, renal disease, etc.
measurementIndicators: CBC/hemoglobin; iron studies; clinical assessment
caveats: Association with cognition does not prove anemia is the sole cause; confounding is substantial.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with nutrition, chronic disease, age, workload, and pregnancy.

name: Autonomic hyperarousal / sympathetic dominance
definition: Elevated sympathetic activation or reduced parasympathetic regulation that persists beyond immediate task needs.
mechanism: Autonomic state influences vigilance, bodily salience, attention, and readiness for action.
behavioralConsequences: Hypervigilance, increased reactivity, difficulty disengaging from threat cues, reduced flexible control in some contexts.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May bias what information is noticed and make calming, reflective, or complex behavioral alternatives harder to implement.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Can arise from stress, stimulants, pain, illness, sleep loss, or anxiety; etiology matters.
measurementIndicators: Heart rate; HRV; electrodermal activity; respiration; blood pressure
caveats: Low HRV or high heart rate alone is not a behavioral diagnosis.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with psychological threat appraisal, stimulants, sleep, and environmental danger.

name: Biological embedding of early-life adversity
definition: Long-lasting physiological alterations associated with severe or chronic early-life adversity, including stress, immune, metabolic, and neural pathways.
mechanism: Early experience can recalibrate HPA-axis, immune, epigenetic, neural, and metabolic systems during sensitive developmental periods.
behavioralConsequences: May alter later stress reactivity, attention, emotion regulation, health, and behavioral vulnerability.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Past context can influence present biological response to interventions; early adversity is not destiny and effects are modifiable.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Human evidence is strongest for broad associations and physiological embedding; specific causal pathways remain under study.
measurementIndicators: Exposure history plus stress, immune, epigenetic, or neurodevelopmental measures in research
caveats: Do not infer trauma history from physiology or claim transgenerational epigenetic determinism.
crossLayerInteractions: A canonical cross-layer bridge from social/environmental exposures to biological regulation.

name: Caffeine withdrawal
definition: Symptoms following abrupt reduction of habitual caffeine consumption.
mechanism: Adenosine-system adaptation produces headache, fatigue, reduced alertness, and concentration difficulty.
behavioralConsequences: Headache, sleepiness, fatigue, low alertness, reduced performance.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can temporarily reduce engagement or performance and confound comparisons of caffeine users vs abstinent controls.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Usually begins within a day and resolves over days; severity depends on habitual intake.
measurementIndicators: Habitual dose; time since last caffeine; withdrawal symptoms
caveats: Withdrawal reversal explains part of caffeine's apparent performance benefit in habitual users.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep, work schedule, stress, and habitual routines.

name: Cannabis withdrawal
definition: Symptoms following cessation or reduction after frequent/prolonged cannabis use.
mechanism: Neuroadaptation of endocannabinoid systems can produce irritability, sleep disturbance, appetite change, and craving.
behavioralConsequences: Irritability, sleep problems, decreased appetite, restlessness, mood symptoms, craving.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Withdrawal can undermine adherence to other changes and temporarily alter sleep/attention.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Severity varies with frequency, dose, THC potency, and comorbidity.
measurementIndicators: Use history; withdrawal scales; time since cessation
caveats: Not all regular users develop clinically meaningful withdrawal.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep, stress, peer context, and other substances.

name: Chronic allostatic load / multisystem stress dysregulation
definition: Cumulative multisystem physiological burden associated with repeated or chronic adaptation to stressors.
mechanism: Repeated stress can alter neuroendocrine, autonomic, immune, metabolic, and cardiovascular regulation.
behavioralConsequences: Associated with poorer health, fatigue, cognitive vulnerability, and reduced adaptive reserve.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can reduce capacity to adopt or maintain new behaviors and change responses to acute stressors.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Most human evidence is observational; allostatic-load indices vary by study.
measurementIndicators: Composite biomarkers: BP, waist/HDL, cortisol, inflammatory markers, autonomic measures
caveats: Do not use as a precise individual causal score without context; indices are not standardized.
crossLayerInteractions: Strongly cross-layer: chronic structural/social adversity can become biologically embedded.

name: Chronic glycemic dysregulation / diabetes-related metabolic burden
definition: Persistent or recurrent abnormal glucose regulation that can affect vascular, neural, and energy systems.
mechanism: Hyperglycemia, vascular injury, insulin resistance, and glycemic variability can affect neural and physical function over time.
behavioralConsequences: Associations with cognitive decline, fatigue, neuropathy, and variable performance; acute extremes can be more directly impairing.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change plans must account for treatment burden, energy variability, neuropathy, and risk of hypo/hyperglycemia.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Causality and magnitude depend on disease duration, control, comorbidities, and age.
measurementIndicators: HbA1c; glucose; CGM metrics; complications; clinical diagnosis
caveats: Do not treat modest glucose fluctuations in healthy people as equivalent to diabetes-related dysfunction.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with medication, diet, stress, sleep, socioeconomic access, and physical activity.

name: Chronic inflammatory burden
definition: Persistently elevated inflammatory activity associated with chronic disease, adiposity, aging, or prolonged stress.
mechanism: Long-term inflammatory signaling can affect energy, vascular and neural function and is associated with cognitive/affective vulnerability.
behavioralConsequences: Fatigue, reduced activity, and associations with cognitive decline or mood symptoms.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May reduce energy available for sustained behavior change and amplify effects of illness or stress.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Causal direction is often uncertain in observational studies.
measurementIndicators: Repeated CRP/IL-6 and clinical inflammatory markers
caveats: Do not use inflammation as a catch-all explanation for complex behavior.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with metabolic status, stress, sleep, aging, and structural adversity.

name: Chronic undernutrition / sustained energy deficiency
definition: Sustained energy and nutrient intake insufficient to meet physiological requirements.
mechanism: Reduced substrate availability and loss of lean mass can impair physical capacity, immune function, and cognitive performance.
behavioralConsequences: Fatigue, reduced strength, impaired concentration and learning in severe or prolonged states.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can reduce capability for sustained behavior change and increase competing need salience.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Human cognitive evidence varies by age, severity, and comorbidity; much evidence is observational.
measurementIndicators: BMI/weight change; dietary assessment; clinical nutrition markers; functional status
caveats: Do not infer individual cognition from body size alone.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with food insecurity, illness, culture, poverty, and physical workload.

name: Chronotype–schedule mismatch / social jetlag
definition: Persistent mismatch between an individual's preferred biological timing and required social/work timing.
mechanism: Mismatch can produce chronic sleep curtailment and repeated circadian misalignment.
behavioralConsequences: Lower alertness at required times, sleep debt, and potentially poorer cognitive/health outcomes.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May affect when people are most receptive to learning, persuasion, complex decisions, or behavior-change demands.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Evidence for specific cognitive effects is heterogeneous and often observational.
measurementIndicators: Morningness-eveningness scales; midsleep timing; social jetlag metrics
caveats: Chronotype is not a personality type and does not dictate behavior.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with age, work schedules, light exposure, family obligations, and technology use.

name: Circadian misalignment / biological-night work
definition: Behavior occurring at a clock time that is misaligned with internal circadian phase, as in night work or rapid schedule shifts.
mechanism: Circadian timing alters arousal, temperature, hormonal rhythms, sleep propensity, and cognitive performance independent of time awake.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced alertness and cognitive performance, increased error risk, altered mood and metabolic regulation.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can make the same behavioral demand substantially harder at biological night; timing of interventions and critical decisions matters.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Night shift, jet lag, rotating schedules, and forced desynchrony; adaptation varies.
measurementIndicators: Dim-light melatonin onset; core body temperature; work schedule; actigraphy
caveats: Shift work includes social and structural factors beyond circadian physiology.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep debt, lighting, work design, meal timing, and social obligations.

name: Clinically meaningful hypoglycemia
definition: Blood glucose low enough to impair normal brain and autonomic function.
mechanism: Reduced glucose availability and counter-regulatory responses can impair attention, speed, executive function, and consciousness as severity increases.
behavioralConsequences: Confusion, slower cognition, impaired coordination/judgment; severe cases can cause loss of consciousness or seizure.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Makes complex behavioral demands unsafe or unrealistic until physiology is corrected.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Most relevant to diabetes treatment, prolonged fasting, or specific metabolic conditions—not ordinary mild hunger.
measurementIndicators: Capillary/venous glucose; continuous glucose monitor; symptom context
caveats: Do not equate normal pre-meal hunger with hypoglycemia.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with medication, food access, exertion, sleep, and stress.

name: Cold strain
definition: Physiological cooling and thermoregulatory activation caused by cold exposure.
mechanism: Peripheral vasoconstriction, shivering, discomfort, and reduced dexterity/nerve conduction can impair performance.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced manual dexterity, attention, endurance, and task efficiency at sufficient cold exposure.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can change willingness and ability to perform precise, prolonged, or exposed behaviors.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Depends on wind, wetness, clothing, acclimatization, body composition, and task.
measurementIndicators: Core/skin temperature; thermal sensation; dexterity/performance measures
caveats: Cold effects differ by body region and task; do not infer broad cognitive impairment from mild discomfort.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with clothing, shelter, workload, and social/organizational requirements.

name: Delirium / acute encephalopathy
definition: Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition caused by medical illness, medication, metabolic disturbance, or other physiological insult.
mechanism: Global brain dysfunction disrupts arousal, attention, orientation, memory, and perception.
behavioralConsequences: Inattention, confusion, disorganized thinking, fluctuating consciousness, altered behavior.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Ordinary persuasion or instruction is unreliable during delirium; treat underlying physiology and ensure safety.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Common in hospitalized/older/critically ill patients; reversible causes should be sought urgently.
measurementIndicators: Clinical delirium screening (CAM/4AT); medical workup
caveats: A medical syndrome, not a normal aging effect or personality issue.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with infection, medication, sleep disruption, sensory loss, and institutional environment.

name: Dyspnea / air hunger
definition: Uncomfortable awareness of breathing difficulty or unmet ventilatory demand.
mechanism: Respiratory/interoceptive signaling generates powerful aversive motivation and threat-related attention.
behavioralConsequences: Activity avoidance, urgency, anxiety-like arousal, reduced cognitive bandwidth, prioritization of breathing/escape.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior change requiring exertion or sustained attention may fail when breathlessness is not addressed.
contextsBoundaryConditions: May reflect cardiopulmonary disease, hypoxia, anxiety, exertion, or environmental exposure.
measurementIndicators: Dyspnea scales; respiratory rate; oxygen saturation; spirometry/context
caveats: Dyspnea is a symptom state, not a diagnosis; psychological interpretation can amplify or reduce distress.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with physical environment, exertion, anxiety, smoke/air quality, and illness.

name: Early-childhood neurodevelopmental stage
definition: Period of rapid brain, language, motor, executive, and socioemotional development in early childhood.
mechanism: Maturing neural systems constrain attention span, inhibition, memory strategies, language comprehension, and learning mechanisms.
behavioralConsequences: Greater dependence on caregivers and context, limited executive control, rapid learning and plasticity.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior change in children relies more on environmental structuring, repetition, modeling, and caregiver-mediated reinforcement than adult-style reasoning.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Development is highly variable; age bands are crude proxies.
measurementIndicators: Developmental assessment; age; language/executive/motor milestones
caveats: Do not treat developmental limitations as deficits or assume all children of the same age are equivalent.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with caregiving, education, culture, nutrition, sleep, and stress.

name: Elevated CO₂ / hypercapnic burden
definition: Increased inspired or arterial carbon dioxide that can alter cerebral physiology and subjective air quality.
mechanism: CO2 changes ventilation and cerebral blood flow; higher levels can cause headache, somnolence, and cognitive impairment.
behavioralConsequences: At clearly hypercapnic levels: impaired alertness and cognition; effects of typical indoor elevations on complex cognition remain debated.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Potentially relevant in poorly ventilated or confined environments, but should not be overstated.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Distinguish clinical hypercapnia from modest indoor CO2 used as a ventilation proxy.
measurementIndicators: Ambient CO2; end-tidal CO2; arterial blood gas
caveats: Evidence for cognitive effects below occupational limits is mixed; CO2 may proxy for other indoor pollutants.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with ventilation, occupancy, respiratory disease, and heat.

name: Focal neurological injury / stroke
driverRole: Capacity constraint / acute or chronic brain state
definition: Focal disruption of brain function from stroke or other localized neurological injury.
mechanism: Lesion location can impair language, attention, memory, motor control, affect, or awareness.
behavioralConsequences: Highly specific deficits such as aphasia, neglect, executive dysfunction, weakness, or impulsivity.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change communication and task design must match preserved abilities and compensate for specific deficits.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend strongly on lesion location, severity, recovery, and rehabilitation.
measurementIndicators: Neurologic exam; imaging; neuropsychological/functional testing
caveats: Do not generalize one deficit profile to all stroke survivors.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with assistive technology, rehabilitation, caregiver support, and built environment.

name: Frailty / accelerated biological aging
definition: State of reduced multisystem physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors, which may diverge from chronological age.
mechanism: Loss of muscle, energy, autonomic/metabolic reserve, and recovery capacity increases cost of adaptation.
behavioralConsequences: Higher fatigue, slower recovery, mobility limitations, vulnerability to acute stressors and hospitalization.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Changes that seem simple may be disproportionately costly; graded support and environmental modification may be necessary.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Frailty constructs vary; often overlaps with chronic disease and social vulnerability.
measurementIndicators: Frailty phenotype/index; gait speed; grip strength; weight loss; exhaustion
caveats: Frailty is not inevitable with age and can be partly modifiable.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with nutrition, institutions, caregiving, environment, and chronic disease.

name: Gene–environment interaction / differential biological susceptibility
definition: Variation in how strongly individuals respond biologically or behaviorally to environmental exposures because of genotype or stable biological differences.
mechanism: Genetic and regulatory variation can alter sensitivity to stressors, rewards, toxins, nutrition, or social environments.
behavioralConsequences: The same exposure can yield different behavioral outcomes across individuals.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Supports tailoring and uncertainty: identical interventions need not have identical effects.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Robust evidence exists for G×E broadly, but specific candidate-gene claims have often failed replication.
measurementIndicators: Large-sample genomic interaction studies; family/twin designs; measured environment
caveats: Avoid candidate-gene storytelling and deterministic personalization.
crossLayerInteractions: Explicitly links biological susceptibility with environmental/social/structural layers.

name: Hearing impairment / degraded auditory input
definition: Reduced auditory sensitivity or clarity that limits access to spoken or environmental information.
mechanism: Degraded sensory input increases listening effort and can reduce communication accuracy and situational awareness.
behavioralConsequences: Missed information, slower communication, greater cognitive effort, social withdrawal or misunderstanding.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change communication may fail if auditory access is poor; redundancy and accessible channels matter.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Severity, hearing aids, noise, language, and cognitive reserve moderate effects.
measurementIndicators: Audiometry; speech-in-noise testing; hearing-device status
caveats: Do not infer low comprehension or cognition from hearing loss.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with information design, social exclusion, age, technology, and environmental noise.

name: Heat strain / hyperthermia
definition: Physiological heat load sufficient to increase core temperature, cardiovascular strain, dehydration, or thermal discomfort.
mechanism: Thermoregulatory demand competes for cardiovascular and attentional resources and increases perceived effort.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced endurance, slower/less accurate cognitive performance under sufficient heat strain, irritability and task disengagement.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavioral interventions requiring sustained effort may fail if thermal strain is not addressed.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend on humidity, acclimatization, hydration, clothing, exertion, and task complexity.
measurementIndicators: Core/skin temperature; heart rate; thermal sensation; WBGT; hydration
caveats: Ambient heat is environmental; heat strain is the biological response.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with hydration, workload, PPE, infrastructure, and sleep.

name: Hunger / acute energy-deficit state
definition: Physiological state associated with energy need and pre-meal hunger signaling.
mechanism: Homeostatic and reward systems increase salience and valuation of food-related cues; ghrelin and related signals participate.
behavioralConsequences: Greater attention to food, altered food choice and valuation; effects on non-food decisions are less consistent.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change demands competing with hunger may lose priority, especially when the target behavior is food-related.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Strongest evidence is domain-specific to food and reward; generalized 'hungry people make bad decisions' claims are weak.
measurementIndicators: Time since meal; hunger ratings; ghrelin; glucose context
caveats: Do not generalize food-domain effects to all risk-taking or morality.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with scarcity, food availability, culture, marketing, and stress.

name: Hypohydration / dehydration
definition: Reduction in total body water sufficient to alter physiological function.
mechanism: Changes in osmolality, cardiovascular strain, thermoregulation, and subjective effort can affect performance.
behavioralConsequences: Physical performance and discomfort are reliably affected at sufficient levels; generic cognitive impairment at moderate levels is less consistently supported.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can make effortful behavior harder and interact with heat/exertion; hydration interventions should not assume broad cognitive enhancement.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Severity, heat, exercise, and baseline hydration determine effects.
measurementIndicators: Body mass change; urine/plasma osmolality; urine specific gravity; fluid balance
caveats: Meta-analytic evidence does not support strong universal cognitive impairment from moderate hypohydration.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with heat, exertion, access, illness, and stimulant/diuretic use.

name: Intermittent hypoxemia / sleep-disordered breathing
definition: Repeated episodes of reduced oxygenation, often during sleep, combined with sleep fragmentation.
mechanism: Intermittent hypoxia and fragmented sleep may impair vigilance, executive function, mood, and cardiovascular regulation.
behavioralConsequences: Daytime sleepiness, attentional instability, reduced executive capacity.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can undermine learning and adherence; treatment may improve daytime function in affected individuals.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Often confounded with obesity, cardiometabolic disease, and sleep fragmentation.
measurementIndicators: Apnea-hypopnea index; overnight oximetry; polysomnography
caveats: Separate effects of hypoxemia from sleep fragmentation are difficult to isolate.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep, obesity/metabolic status, age, and medications.

name: Intrusive tinnitus / persistent internal auditory signal
definition: Persistent perception of sound without a corresponding external source, when sufficiently salient or distressing to compete for attention.
mechanism: Persistent auditory percept can consume attentional resources and interact with sleep, affect, and executive control.
behavioralConsequences: Associations with poorer executive function, processing speed, memory, and selective attention; distress varies widely.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May reduce concentration or learning capacity and make quiet environments paradoxically more difficult for some people.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend on severity, hearing loss, sleep, anxiety/depression, and distress.
measurementIndicators: Tinnitus severity/handicap scales; audiology; cognitive testing
caveats: Many people with tinnitus function normally; avoid treating tinnitus as a uniform cognitive deficit.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with hearing loss, sleep, stress, and environmental sound.

name: Iron deficiency
definition: Insufficient iron stores, with or without anemia, affecting oxygen transport and iron-dependent neural processes.
mechanism: Iron participates in hemoglobin, myelination, and neurotransmitter-related enzymes; deficiency can impair energy and development.
behavioralConsequences: Fatigue and, especially in developmental periods, learning/attention vulnerability.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Correcting true deficiency can improve capacity; supplementation in iron-replete people should not be treated as a cognitive enhancer.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Behavioral evidence differs by age, severity, and presence of anemia.
measurementIndicators: Ferritin; transferrin saturation; hemoglobin; clinical assessment
caveats: Avoid generic supplement claims; diagnose deficiency.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with diet, menstruation/pregnancy, chronic disease, and socioeconomic access.

name: Medication / polypharmacy cognitive-sedative burden
definition: Combined cognitive, sedative, anticholinergic, orthostatic, or motor effects arising from multiple medications or high-risk medication classes.
mechanism: Additive or interacting drug effects can reduce arousal, memory, balance, reaction speed, or executive function, especially in vulnerable adults.
behavioralConsequences: Sedation, attention/memory difficulty, falls risk, slower behavior, reduced adherence complexity and treatment burden.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Observed nonadherence or low engagement may reflect medication burden or regimen complexity rather than motivation alone.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Most evidence is strongest in older adults; confounding by illness severity and indication is substantial.
measurementIndicators: Medication reconciliation; anticholinergic/sedative burden scales; timing; cognitive/functional assessment
caveats: Polypharmacy itself is not always harmful; medication appropriateness and specific pharmacology matter. Never imply medication changes without clinical review.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with age, neurological status, sleep, substance use, healthcare access, and regimen complexity.

name: Menstrual-cycle hormonal phase
definition: Normal cyclic variation in ovarian hormones across the menstrual cycle.
mechanism: Estradiol/progesterone variations affect multiple neural and physiological systems, but average cognitive effects in healthy adults are small/inconsistent.
behavioralConsequences: Some individuals experience symptom-related changes in pain, mood, sleep, or energy; robust general cognitive impairment is not supported.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May matter for symptom-sensitive behaviors in specific individuals, but should not be assumed as a population-wide driver.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Large individual differences and methodological limitations.
measurementIndicators: Cycle phase; symptom tracking; hormonal confirmation in research
caveats: Strong caution: do not use menstrual phase to stereotype competence or decision quality.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with pain, sleep, culture, work demands, and individual symptom burden.

name: Mental / cognitive fatigue
definition: Psychobiological state following prolonged demanding cognitive activity, characterized by weariness and reduced willingness or ability to sustain control.
mechanism: Sustained cognitive control changes neural/metabolic and motivational processes, increasing effort cost.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced vigilance, slower or less accurate cognition, greater disengagement; can reduce subsequent physical endurance.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Complex behavior-change tasks may need simplification, breaks, automation, or timing away from high cognitive load.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Task duration and individual expectations affect magnitude.
measurementIndicators: Time-on-task; performance decline; fatigue scales; pupillometry/EEG/fMRI in research
caveats: Do not equate mental fatigue with generic lack of motivation or 'ego depletion'.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with workload, sleep loss, stress, interface design, and incentives.

name: Metabolic reserve / chronic metabolic disease burden
definition: Reduced physiological flexibility or reserve associated with chronic metabolic disease, obesity-related complications, or multimorbidity.
mechanism: Metabolic, vascular, inflammatory, and mechanical pathways can increase fatigue and constrain activity.
behavioralConsequences: Higher effort cost, reduced endurance, sleep-disordered breathing risk, and possible cognitive vulnerability.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May affect feasibility and persistence of physically or cognitively demanding changes.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Body weight alone is not a sufficient measure; disease burden and function matter.
measurementIndicators: Clinical metabolic profile; functional testing; comorbidity measures
caveats: Avoid weight-essentialist or stigmatizing causal claims.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with environment, food access, stigma, sleep, inflammation, and institutional healthcare.

name: Mild traumatic brain injury / concussion state
definition: Transient or persistent neurobehavioral effects following mild traumatic brain injury.
mechanism: Neurometabolic, vestibular, sensory, sleep, and network disturbances can affect cognition and symptom tolerance.
behavioralConsequences: Headache, slowed processing, attention/memory problems, fatigue, dizziness, irritability; recovery is usually favorable but variable.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Complex learning, multitasking, or high-stimulation environments may need temporary modification.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Symptoms overlap with pain, sleep, stress, and vestibular dysfunction.
measurementIndicators: Clinical concussion assessment; symptom scales; neurocognitive/vestibular testing
caveats: Do not infer permanent impairment from concussion; prognosis varies and many recover fully.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep, pain, vestibular function, stress, work demands, and information load.

name: Moderate/severe TBI sequelae
definition: Persistent cognitive, emotional, behavioral, or motor consequences after moderate or severe traumatic brain injury.
mechanism: Diffuse/focal neural injury can impair executive functions, memory, inhibition, social cognition, and motor systems.
behavioralConsequences: Executive dysfunction, impulsivity, memory problems, reduced initiation, motor limitations.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior change may require external structure, cueing, simplified choices, repetition, and caregiver/system support.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Profiles vary greatly by lesion, recovery, premorbid function, and rehabilitation.
measurementIndicators: Neuropsychological testing; imaging; functional assessments
caveats: Avoid treating TBI as a uniform personality change.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with social support, rehabilitation, substance use, institutions, and technology aids.

name: Nausea / visceral malaise
definition: Aversive interoceptive state signaling gastrointestinal or systemic disturbance.
mechanism: Brainstem, vagal, vestibular, and interoceptive pathways generate avoidance motivation and attentional capture.
behavioralConsequences: Withdrawal from activity, reduced appetite, avoidance, difficulty concentrating, altered risk/effort tolerance.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can dominate motivation and reduce willingness to engage in tasks, travel, learning, or interventions.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Etiology matters: illness, medication, motion sickness, toxins, pregnancy, anxiety.
measurementIndicators: Symptom scales; emesis; trigger context; clinical measures as appropriate
caveats: Behavioral consequences are plausible and strong, but direct causal studies of complex decision-making are limited.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with vestibular state, pregnancy, medication, stress, and environment.

name: Neurodegenerative disease burden
definition: Progressive neural degeneration that can impair memory, executive control, language, movement, or social cognition.
mechanism: Disease-specific neural loss and network dysfunction progressively alter cognitive and motor capacities.
behavioralConsequences: Changes in memory, judgment, initiation, inhibition, language, navigation, or motor function depending on disease.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior change often requires environmental redesign, cueing, caregiver support, and reduced cognitive complexity.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Disease types and stages differ substantially; healthy aging is separate.
measurementIndicators: Clinical diagnosis; neuropsychology; imaging/biomarkers as appropriate; functional status
caveats: Avoid equating older age with neurodegeneration.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with social care, technology, medication, sensory impairment, and institutional context.

name: Nicotine withdrawal
definition: Physiological and cognitive symptoms following cessation or reduction of nicotine in a dependent user.
mechanism: Neuroadaptation to chronic nicotinic stimulation produces withdrawal-related changes in attention, mood, and reward.
behavioralConsequences: Irritability, craving, concentration difficulty, reduced attention/working memory, restlessness.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Withdrawal can dominate short-term behavior and make unrelated behavior-change tasks harder; cessation support can reduce the barrier.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Severity depends on dependence level, time since last use, and replacement therapy.
measurementIndicators: Time since nicotine; dependence scales; withdrawal scales
caveats: Some apparent 'cognitive enhancement' from nicotine in smokers is withdrawal reversal.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with stress, cues, social environment, and access to nicotine replacement.

name: Normative biological aging
definition: Age-associated changes in neural processing speed, sensory systems, sleep, cardiovascular function, and physiological reserve.
mechanism: Gradual changes in brain and body systems alter speed, memory, sensory input, and tolerance for physiological stressors.
behavioralConsequences: Slower processing and some memory changes on average, with preserved or improved knowledge in other domains; large individual variability.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change materials may need accessible sensory design, pacing, and support for working memory/complexity.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Healthy aging differs from MCI, dementia, frailty, or disease.
measurementIndicators: Age plus cognitive, sensory, and functional assessment
caveats: Chronological age alone is a weak individual predictor; avoid ageism.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sensory loss, medication, health, technology familiarity, and social structure.

name: Olfactory impairment
definition: Reduced ability to detect or identify odors.
mechanism: Loss of olfactory sensory input reduces detection of food, smoke, gas, spoilage, and socially meaningful odor cues.
behavioralConsequences: Altered food enjoyment/intake, reduced hazard detection, changes in quality of life.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can alter nutrition-related behavior and safety responses; may also be a marker of neurological disease.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Direct effects on complex social behavior are less well established.
measurementIndicators: Odor identification/detection testing; self-report
caveats: Do not infer neurodegenerative disease from olfactory loss alone.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with food environment, safety systems, illness, and aging.

name: Opioid intoxication / opioid-related CNS depression
definition: Acute CNS effects of opioid agonists, ranging from analgesia to sedation and respiratory depression depending on dose/tolerance.
mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activation alters pain, reward, arousal, respiration, and psychomotor function.
behavioralConsequences: Sedation, slowed reaction and attention; at high dose, respiratory depression and loss of consciousness.
behaviorChangeRelevance: High-stakes decisions or tasks may be impaired during sedation; analgesia can simultaneously improve function by reducing pain.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects depend heavily on dose, tolerance, pain state, chronic use, and co-sedatives.
measurementIndicators: Medication/dose/time; sedation score; respiratory rate; toxicology context
caveats: Chronic prescribed opioid use does not uniformly cause major cognitive impairment; pain relief can improve function.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with pain, benzodiazepines/alcohol, respiratory disease, and dependence.

name: Opioid withdrawal
definition: Physiological syndrome following abrupt reduction or antagonism of opioids in a dependent person.
mechanism: Noradrenergic and other neuroadaptations produce severe autonomic, gastrointestinal, pain, and craving symptoms.
behavioralConsequences: Restlessness, pain, diarrhea, nausea, dysphoria, craving, sleep disruption and strong drug-seeking motivation.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Competing behavioral goals may be overwhelmed by withdrawal; evidence-based treatment substantially changes the behavioral landscape.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Severity depends on opioid type, dose, duration, and treatment status.
measurementIndicators: Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale; use history; vitals; symptoms
caveats: Withdrawal is highly aversive but usually not life-threatening; treatment access is a structural factor.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with pain, social context, treatment access, stigma, and cues.

name: Overt thyroid hormone dysregulation
definition: Clinically significant hypo- or hyperthyroidism producing systemic metabolic and neurological effects.
mechanism: Thyroid hormones regulate metabolism, cardiovascular function, arousal, and neural processes.
behavioralConsequences: Fatigue/slowing with hypothyroidism; hyperarousal, tremor, sleep disruption or concentration difficulty with hyperthyroidism.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior and learning may be affected when overt disease is untreated; treatment can remove a biological constraint.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Subclinical thyroid abnormalities show inconsistent cognitive associations.
measurementIndicators: TSH, free T4/T3, clinical symptoms
caveats: Do not use minor lab variation as a behavioral explanation; subclinical effects are uncertain.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep, mood, cardiovascular state, medication, and age.

name: Perimenopausal / menopausal transition
definition: Transition involving fluctuating and declining ovarian hormones with changes in thermoregulation, sleep, and other physiological systems.
mechanism: Hormonal variability and vasomotor/sleep disturbance may influence attention, memory complaints, and energy.
behavioralConsequences: Hot flashes, sleep disruption, fatigue, and modest cognitive changes for some individuals.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change programs may need to address sleep/thermal symptoms and timing rather than assume motivational causes.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Average cognitive effects are generally modest and heterogeneous.
measurementIndicators: Menopausal stage; symptom scales; sleep; clinical hormone measures when indicated
caveats: Do not treat menopause as cognitive decline; many effects are small and mediated by symptoms.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep, stress, work environment, culture, and aging.

name: Persistent / chronic pain burden
definition: Ongoing or recurrent pain lasting beyond normal tissue healing that can alter attention, sleep, movement, and cognition.
mechanism: Persistent nociceptive/salience processing plus sleep disruption and reduced activity can burden executive and attentional systems.
behavioralConsequences: Avoidance, reduced activity, attentional capture, executive-function difficulties, altered reward/effort valuation.
behaviorChangeRelevance: New behaviors may need reduced physical/cognitive cost and attention to pain-related avoidance or energy limits.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Comorbid sleep disturbance, depression, medication, and disability confound many associations.
measurementIndicators: Pain interference; disability scales; quantitative sensory testing; activity measures
caveats: Chronic pain is heterogeneous; avoid assuming cognitive deficits in every individual.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with medication, sleep, mood, work structure, mobility, and social support.

name: Physical / exertional fatigue
definition: Reduced capacity or increased effort following sustained or intense physical work.
mechanism: Peripheral and central fatigue processes increase perceived effort and reduce motor output and persistence.
behavioralConsequences: Lower endurance, slower movement, reduced precision, altered pacing and willingness to continue.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior change that requires physical effort is less likely when effort cost is elevated.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects on cognitive performance are heterogeneous; distinguish physical from mental fatigue.
measurementIndicators: Performance decrement; RPE; force/power; physiological workload
caveats: Fatigue is task-specific and multifactorial; subjective fatigue and performance fatigability are not identical.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with heat, sleep, nutrition, pain, motivation, and equipment.

name: Polygenic / heritable predisposition
definition: Small effects from many genetic variants that contribute probabilistically to behavioral traits or vulnerabilities at the population level.
mechanism: Polygenic variation influences neural, endocrine, metabolic, and developmental pathways that interact with environments.
behavioralConsequences: Shifts probabilities or trait distributions rather than directly specifying complex behavior.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Useful as a background susceptibility concept, not a proximate intervention target in ordinary behavior-change practice.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Predictive power varies greatly across traits and populations and is often ancestry-dependent.
measurementIndicators: Genotyping/polygenic scores in research; family/twin designs at population level
caveats: Heritability is not immutability; polygenic scores are not causal explanations of individual behavior.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with nearly every layer through gene–environment correlation and interaction.

name: Post-infectious / convalescent fatigue state
definition: Persistent fatigue and reduced capacity after an acute infection has otherwise resolved.
mechanism: Multiple mechanisms may contribute, including immune dysregulation, autonomic changes, sleep disturbance, and deconditioning.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced endurance, slower recovery, cognitive fatigue, activity limitation.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change expectations may need pacing and graded capacity assessment rather than assuming resistance.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Mechanisms and duration vary widely by pathogen and individual.
measurementIndicators: Fatigue scales; activity; functional tests; clinical workup
caveats: Heterogeneous and not specific to any one diagnosis; avoid unsupported mechanistic certainty.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with employment demands, social expectations, sleep, and physical conditioning.

name: Pregnancy physiological/endocrine state
definition: Pregnancy-related endocrine, cardiovascular, metabolic, immune, and sleep changes.
mechanism: Large hormonal and physiological shifts affect sleep, fatigue, nausea, thermoregulation, and some cognitive domains.
behavioralConsequences: Fatigue, nausea, altered sleep, physical capacity changes; meta-analytic evidence suggests modest cognitive differences in some domains.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change demands should account for changing energy, symptoms, risk constraints, and physical capability.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects vary by trimester, symptom burden, parity, sleep, and individual.
measurementIndicators: Pregnancy stage; symptom measures; clinical markers
caveats: Avoid stereotypes such as universal 'pregnancy brain'; average effects are modest and heterogeneous.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with work policy, caregiving, nutrition, social support, and medical risk.

name: Prolonged stress recovery / sustained physiological activation
definition: Slow return of physiological stress systems toward baseline after a challenge.
mechanism: Extended cortisol/autonomic activation increases physiological load and can prolong attentional and emotional consequences of stress.
behavioralConsequences: Longer persistence of threat-focused processing, fatigue, irritability, and reduced flexibility after an event.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can prolong windows in which messages, decisions, or social interactions are processed under altered physiological conditions.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Recovery trajectories vary substantially among individuals and stressor types.
measurementIndicators: Post-stressor cortisol/HRV recovery slope; repeated physiological sampling
caveats: Recovery is not equivalent to subjective calm and is difficult to infer without repeated measurement.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with social support, controllability, sleep, prior stress exposure, and coping.

name: Pubertal endocrine transition
definition: Coordinated gonadal and adrenal hormonal maturation during puberty interacting with brain and social development.
mechanism: Pubertal hormones influence reward, social salience, body maturation, sleep timing, and stress systems.
behavioralConsequences: Changes in social motivation, reward sensitivity, sleep timing, and risk behavior occur alongside neural/social development.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change approaches for adolescents should account for developmental reward/social sensitivity rather than assume adult motivational architecture.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Hormones are only one contributor; peer context and brain maturation are critical.
measurementIndicators: Pubertal stage; age; hormonal assays in research
caveats: Avoid 'hormones make teens reckless' explanations; effects are probabilistic and context-dependent.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with social status, peers, culture, sleep phase, and institutional autonomy.

name: Reduced mobility / physical reserve / frailty
definition: Reduced physiological reserve, strength, balance, or mobility that increases the effort and risk of everyday action.
mechanism: Lower musculoskeletal and cardiopulmonary reserve makes behaviors more energetically costly and recovery slower.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced activity, slower movement, greater fall avoidance, lower tolerance for demanding tasks.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change plans must account for actual physical capability and effort cost rather than assuming motivation failure.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Common in aging/chronic illness but not exclusive to older adults.
measurementIndicators: Gait speed; grip strength; chair-rise; frailty indices; ADL/IADL measures
caveats: Frailty is multidimensional and partially shaped by social/environmental conditions.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with built environment, access, caregiving, chronic disease, and age.

name: Repeated partial sleep restriction
definition: Obtaining less sleep than physiologically needed across multiple consecutive nights.
mechanism: Cumulative sleep debt degrades sustained attention, processing efficiency, working memory, and executive function.
behavioralConsequences: Progressive vigilance lapses, reduced cognitive throughput, poorer learning and error monitoring.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can gradually erode intervention adherence, training uptake, decision quality, and persistence even when people report adapting.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Magnitude depends on nightly sleep opportunity, baseline sleep need, recovery sleep, and task demands.
measurementIndicators: Sleep diary; actigraphy; sleep duration; PVT; fatigue scales
caveats: Subjective sleepiness may underestimate objective performance decline.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with shift work, caregiving, operations tempo, family structure, and organizational schedules.

name: Satiety / postprandial state
definition: Physiological state following food intake characterized by reduced hunger and altered metabolic/endocrine signals.
mechanism: Gut-brain and metabolic signals reduce food reward and can alter arousal or post-meal alertness.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced food seeking; possible transient changes in alertness depending on meal size/composition.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can shift responsiveness to food incentives and timing of dietary behavior-change efforts.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects on non-food cognition are variable and meal-composition dependent.
measurementIndicators: Meal timing/composition; satiety ratings; glucose/insulin when relevant
caveats: Avoid claims that eating generally improves or worsens decision-making.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with cultural meal patterns, food environment, sleep, and metabolic health.

name: Sedative-hypnotic / benzodiazepine state
definition: Acute or ongoing CNS depressant effects from benzodiazepines or related sedating medications.
mechanism: GABAergic potentiation reduces arousal, reaction speed, memory encoding, and psychomotor coordination.
behavioralConsequences: Sedation, slowed reaction, anterograde memory impairment, balance problems and cognitive slowing.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May make learning and high-precision behaviors unreliable; medication timing should be considered.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects vary by agent, half-life, dose, tolerance, age, and concurrent substances.
measurementIndicators: Medication list; dose/time; clinical sedation/psychomotor assessment
caveats: Long-term cognitive causality is more uncertain than acute impairment; do not stop medications without medical guidance.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with age, alcohol/opioids, sleep, falls risk, and polypharmacy.

name: Seizure / postictal state
definition: Transient period during or after epileptic seizure in which cognition, arousal, memory, language, or behavior may be altered.
mechanism: Abnormal neural activity and postictal network suppression/disorganization temporarily impair function.
behavioralConsequences: Confusion, amnesia, fatigue, language or focal deficits, behavioral disorganization.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Critical instructions and consent/decision demands should account for temporary postictal impairment.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Manifestation varies by seizure type and brain region.
measurementIndicators: Clinical observation; EEG; seizure history; neurologic exam
caveats: Postictal behavior is not a stable disposition.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep loss, medication adherence, stress, and safety environment.

name: Sexual arousal / reproductive motivational state
definition: Physiological and motivational state associated with sexual arousal and reproductive cues.
mechanism: Reward, autonomic, endocrine, and attentional systems increase salience of sexual cues and alter valuation.
behavioralConsequences: Attention and choice can shift toward sexual/reproductive incentives; risk tradeoffs may change in context.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can alter message salience and decision context but is highly situation-specific.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Most evidence concerns specific sexual contexts; not a general behavior driver.
measurementIndicators: Self-report arousal; physiological measures in research
caveats: Do not reduce sexual or social behavior to testosterone or a single hormone.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with culture, relationship context, norms, identity, alcohol/drugs, and opportunity.

name: Sleep fragmentation / poor sleep continuity
definition: Repeated awakenings or disrupted sleep architecture that reduces restorative sleep even when total time in bed appears adequate.
mechanism: Fragmented sleep alters restorative processes and can reduce daytime attention, memory consolidation, and alertness.
behavioralConsequences: Daytime sleepiness, reduced concentration, poorer memory and performance stability.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May weaken learning, implementation of new routines, and sustained adherence by reducing cognitive capacity and energy.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Common causes include sleep apnea, pain, caregiving, noise, and insomnia; cause matters for intervention.
measurementIndicators: Polysomnography; actigraphy; wake after sleep onset; sleep efficiency; apnea indices
caveats: Fragmentation is heterogeneous; avoid treating self-reported poor sleep as equivalent to objectively fragmented sleep.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with environmental noise, pain, respiratory physiology, stress, and age.

name: Sleep inertia
definition: Transient impairment immediately after awakening, especially from deep sleep or at adverse circadian phases.
mechanism: Incomplete restoration of alertness networks after waking causes slowed cognition and impaired vigilance.
behavioralConsequences: Reduced reaction speed, working memory, attention, and decision efficiency after awakening.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Critical alerts or instructions delivered immediately after awakening may be misunderstood, delayed, or poorly executed.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Severity depends on sleep stage, prior sleep deprivation, circadian phase, and nap duration.
measurementIndicators: Time since awakening; performance tests; subjective alertness
caveats: Usually transient; avoid treating it as a stable trait.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with alarms, emergency response, night operations, and sleep restriction.

name: Somatosensory / proprioceptive impairment
definition: Reduced tactile or position-sense information needed for coordinated movement and object interaction.
mechanism: Peripheral nerve, spinal, or central sensory impairment degrades feedback used for motor control and body awareness.
behavioralConsequences: Slower or less accurate movement, increased reliance on vision, fall risk, difficulty manipulating objects.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can make seemingly simple behaviors physically difficult and increase dependence on environmental supports.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Often occurs with neuropathy, injury, aging, or neurological disease.
measurementIndicators: Clinical sensory testing; proprioception; vibration/monofilament; motor tasks
caveats: Behavioral impact is strongly task-dependent.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with lighting, footwear, interface design, mobility aids, and neurological state.

name: Stable individual physiological vulnerability to sleep/stress/load
definition: Relatively repeatable individual differences in performance degradation under sleep loss, stress, heat, or other physiological challenges.
mechanism: Trait-like differences in regulatory systems, sleep need, autonomic/endocrine reactivity, and resilience change response to exposure.
behavioralConsequences: Some individuals show larger performance or behavioral changes than others under equivalent physiological load.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Behavior-change systems should include monitoring and adaptive support rather than assume a uniform exposure-response curve.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Mechanisms are often multifactorial and partly genetic/learned.
measurementIndicators: Repeated challenge testing; longitudinal performance; physiological reactivity profiles
caveats: Vulnerability is domain-specific and should not be generalized across all stressors.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with training, experience, genetics, health, and organizational selection.

name: Stimulant / amphetamine-like pharmacologic state
definition: Acute catecholaminergic stimulation from prescription or nonmedical stimulants.
mechanism: Increases dopamine/norepinephrine signaling, arousal, wakefulness, and task engagement, with dose-dependent costs.
behavioralConsequences: Improved alertness/attention in some contexts; high doses can produce anxiety, perseveration, impulsivity, insomnia, or psychosis.
behaviorChangeRelevance: May increase task persistence but can distort confidence or degrade flexible decision-making at high doses.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Therapeutic ADHD treatment differs from nonmedical/high-dose use.
measurementIndicators: Medication/dose/time; clinical observation; toxicology with context
caveats: Do not generalize therapeutic benefits in diagnosed populations to enhancement in healthy users.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with sleep, stress, cardiovascular state, incentives, and other substances.

name: Stress-system hypo-reactivity / blunted response after chronic adversity
definition: Reduced physiological response to acute challenge observed in some chronically stressed or adversity-exposed populations.
mechanism: Long-term recalibration of HPA/autonomic systems may produce altered threat and reward responsiveness.
behavioralConsequences: May be associated with altered motivation, affective responsiveness, and stress-related behavior, but effects are heterogeneous.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Potentially relevant when a person appears behaviorally unresponsive to stressors that strongly affect others.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Evidence varies by exposure, developmental timing, disorder status, and measurement method.
measurementIndicators: Cortisol or autonomic reactivity to standardized challenge
caveats: Not a universal consequence of trauma or chronic stress; avoid diagnostic inference.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with early-life adversity, social environment, mental health, and genetics.

name: Thirst
definition: Motivational state arising from osmotic/volume signals that drive fluid seeking.
mechanism: Hypothalamic and interoceptive signaling increases salience and motivational value of drinking-related cues.
behavioralConsequences: Fluid-seeking motivation, attentional capture by thirst, altered effort allocation.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Competing behavioral demands may be deprioritized when thirst is strong; access and prompt timing matter.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Thirst can occur before clinically meaningful dehydration.
measurementIndicators: Thirst ratings; serum/plasma osmolality; fluid intake context
caveats: Thirst and dehydration are related but not synonymous.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with heat, exertion, access to water, norms, and operational constraints.

name: Vestibular dysfunction / motion-sickness susceptibility
definition: Disturbance of balance and spatial-orientation systems, including acute motion sickness or chronic vestibular disease.
mechanism: Vestibular signals interact with visual, proprioceptive, autonomic, and hippocampal systems supporting balance and spatial cognition.
behavioralConsequences: Dizziness, nausea, avoidance of movement, balance problems, and visuospatial cognitive difficulty.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can strongly constrain travel, training environments, virtual-reality exposure, and tasks requiring movement or spatial orientation.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Effects vary across vestibular disorders; cognitive evidence is largely associative.
measurementIndicators: Vestibular testing; balance; symptom scales; motion-sickness susceptibility
caveats: Separate vestibular effects from anxiety, hearing loss, medication, and age.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with technology/VR, transportation, visual environment, anxiety, and nausea.

name: Visceral urgency / elimination need
definition: Strong bladder or bowel interoceptive signals that create an immediate need for elimination.
mechanism: Visceral afferent signaling captures attention and increases motivation to terminate competing tasks.
behavioralConsequences: Distraction, haste, avoidance of contexts without facilities, shortened persistence.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Can materially alter compliance, route choice, meeting duration, or attention even when externally invisible.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Evidence for effects on complex decisions is limited; most relevance is mechanistic and situational.
measurementIndicators: Self-report urgency; time since voiding; clinical urodynamic/GI measures when relevant
caveats: Treat as a context-dependent competing need, not a general behavioral trait.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with infrastructure, privacy norms, disability, medication, and time pressure.

name: Visual impairment / degraded visual input
definition: Reduced visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, field, or other visual function that constrains access to visual information.
mechanism: Reduced sensory input increases effort and can impair navigation, reading, object recognition, and hazard detection.
behavioralConsequences: Missed cues, slower information uptake, navigation difficulty, reduced independence or confidence.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Visual behavior-change materials may be ineffective without accessible contrast, size, and alternate channels.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Type of impairment matters; acuity alone may not capture function.
measurementIndicators: Visual acuity; contrast sensitivity; field testing; functional vision
caveats: Associations with cognition may reflect shared causes; visual impairment itself should be treated as access/capability.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with interface design, lighting, built environment, age, and literacy.

name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
definition: Clinically meaningful cobalamin deficiency capable of causing neurological or hematologic dysfunction.
mechanism: B12 is required for myelin and one-carbon metabolism; deficiency can produce neuropathy and cognitive/neuropsychiatric symptoms.
behavioralConsequences: Neurological symptoms, sensory change, fatigue, cognitive impairment in sufficiently deficient cases.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Identification and correction of actual deficiency can remove a biological barrier to behavior and learning.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Supplementation in non-deficient people has not shown reliable cognitive benefit.
measurementIndicators: Serum B12 with MMA/homocysteine as clinically appropriate; CBC; neurologic exam
caveats: Deficiency is a driver; 'B12 boosts cognition' in replete populations is not supported.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with diet, malabsorption, medication, aging, and sensory impairment.

name: Young-adult maturation of executive/control systems
definition: Continued maturation and stabilization of executive, planning, and self-regulatory capacities into early adulthood.
mechanism: Structural/functional brain development and accumulated experience improve some control and planning processes.
behavioralConsequences: On average, increasing consistency in planning, inhibition, and long-horizon behavior compared with adolescence.
behaviorChangeRelevance: Transition points such as military service, university, or workforce entry may combine biological maturation with major environmental change.
contextsBoundaryConditions: Developmental trajectories are gradual and heterogeneous; social role changes are confounded.
measurementIndicators: Age; longitudinal executive-function measures; neuroimaging in research
caveats: Do not assign a precise age at which the 'brain becomes adult'.
crossLayerInteractions: Interacts with education, responsibility, sleep, substance use, and social roles.
